docs.title: Malachite — A Story Format for Twee3
docs.text:
WIP

This documentation is a heavy work in progress. Most sections are still missing or incomplete. However, I am not accepting contributions at this time, as this is a personal project, still in the early stages. Please check back another time!

docs.title: Welcome to Malachite!
docs.text: This is the official documentation for Malachite, an advanced (though not minimal) story format for twine/twee3.

docs.title: Where to go?
docs.text:
1. Before getting started with Malachite, please read the format's About Page! It covers some very important topics and gotchas with the project in its current state.
  2. After you've read the above, head to Installation to get started.
  3. The sidebar includes all important concepts and APIs available with Malachite.

docs.title: About Malachite
docs.text: This page contains some general information about Malachite (as a story format).

docs.title: Why Malachite?
docs.text:
There are plenty of official, well-documented story formats for twine/twee. I would not recommend developing a project with Malachite unless you have ran into multiple of the same pain points as I have:

  • Your project requires a Complex UI with multiple separate passages displayed at the same time, each with a separate history.

    Most twine story formats are built on the assumption that only a single passage will be visible on the screen at any given time. While most formats do have functionality for embedding other passages inside that main passage, Malachite allows for multiple "windows" (AKA frames) to be present, each with a separate history.

  • You are familiar with HTML and javascript and find most abstractions away from this annoying to work with.

    Malachite is very light on the markup and heavy on the javascript. Most of Malachite's interactivity is built on top of Alpine.js, a lightweight javascript framework that already has functionality like conditionals and looping built in.

    Please check out at least the first few pages of Alpine's documentation, it will help you understand Malachite as well.

  • Your project requires a good amount of reactivity with minimum hassle.

    TBA later. Tl;dr Alpine includes reactivity out of the box. Update a variable and it instantly ripples through the entire UI.

  • You need more functionality than a minimal story format out of the box.

    Malchite is not (or at least, won't be) a minimal story format. There will be helper utilities and APIs for things commonly utilized in Interactive Fiction. Examples include crossfading, playing audio and storylets/quality based narratives.

Even then, Malachite is still in heavy development and very unstable, not to mention (mostly) undocumented. Please do not expect this story format to be production ready in any reasonable timeframe, as this is a hobby project of a single developer right now.

docs.title: Why shouldn't I use Malachite?
docs.text:
I highly suggest you do not use this story format in its current state.

There's a couple of reasons, the most important ones being...

  1. Malachite is not production ready. It will not be for a long time.
  2. In addition, prior to v1.0, I will not be providing community support for it. You are on your own.
  3. Malachite is currently heavily undocumented, though (as you can see), efforts are underway to change this.

There are also some other major dealbreakers.

  1. This format is currently only being tested with twee/tweego. Not Twine or any other twee compilers.
  2. There is also no syntax highlighting for either twine or twee/tweego.
  3. This format is fairly advanced. Common twine concepts are often handled differently.

TBA later.

docs.title: Frame Directive
docs.text: Creates a Frame and initializes the contents with the passage specified.

docs.title: x-frame="passage name"
docs.text:
Like the passage directive, you can pass anything that resolves to a valid passage name. 

<div x-frame="'passage name'">
</div>
The passage passed to x-frame will be rendered on frame initialization, unless another passage is already pressent in the State

Tip

Frames get initialized per element, not per name. Meaning each time an element with x-frame appears on the screen, that element will be initialized. In the future, it will be possible to configure default behavior per-name using the Config API.

docs.title: x-frame:name="passage name"
docs.text:
All x-frame directives reference the unnamed frame by default. To use a different frame, you can specify a name by adding a colon and the name of the frame. 

<div x-frame:menu="'Inventory Menu'">
</div>
This assigns the parent div to a frame called "menu".

docs.title: Modifiers
docs.text: The following modifiers are available for x-frame.

docs.title: .overwrite
docs.text:
Usage: x-frame:name.overwrite="passage name"

Makes the default passage always render upon frame initialization, ignoring any current state.

docs.title: Link Directive
docs.text: Swaps the target frame to the passage specified, through altering the frame's state.

docs.title: Link Markup
docs.text:
Standard Twine Link Markup gets transformed into an x-link directive under the hood. I.e. [[Go into the dark->The Dark][quest]] will be rendered as the following: 

<button x-link:quest="'The Dark'">Go into the dark</button>
Using x-link directly offers you the ability to style and customize the link however you want, at the cost of syntax convenience.

docs.title: x-link="passage name"
docs.text:
You can pass anything that resolves to a valid passage name. 

<button x-link="'Next Up'">Go to the next passage!</button>
Like the frame directive, links target the unnamed frame by default.

Tip

It is advised to use x-link on exclusively button elements. It is the easiest way to keep accessibility features (keyboard navigation, etc) functioning as they should.

docs.title: x-link:frame="passage name"
docs.text:
To target another frame, add a colon and the name of the frame. 

<button x-link:menu="'Quest Menu'">Open Quest Log</button>
This will target any frames named "menu".

docs.title: Modifiers
docs.text: The following modifiers are available for the x-link directive.

docs.title: .!play
docs.text:
Usage: x-link.!play="passage name"

Prevents the new state from being pushed to the history.

docs.title: .!fade
docs.text:
Usage: x-link.!fade="passage name"

Prevents the target frame from fading in and out when the link is clicked.

docs.title: Passage Directive
docs.text:
Embeds one passage directly into another. Input must resolve to a valid passage name.

Embedded passages can read data from its parents, enabling widget-like functionality. It is also possible to directly embed html contents into the passage using x-contents.

docs.title: x-passage="passage name"
docs.text:
Tip

The expression inside the double quotes MUST resolve to a string! When passing a simple passage name, a common mistake is to not include the 'single quotes' around the name.

Passing a passage name as a string 

<div x-passage="'passage name'">
</div>

Passing a variable that resolves to a passage name. 

<div x-data="{ title: 'Another Passage' }">
  <!-- resolves to "Another Passage" -->
  <div x-passage="title"></div>
</div>

docs.title: Passing Data
docs.text:
Say we have a passage as described here. 

:: Dialogue Box
<div>
  <b :style="{ color: nameColor }" >{{name}}</b>
  <p>{{dialogue}}</p>
</div>
We can re-use this passage inside another by using x-passage. In order to set each variable used here, we use x-data. 
<div
  x-passage="'Dialogue Box'"
  x-data="{
    name: 'Steve',
    dialogue: 'Hi there!',
    nameColor: 'red'
  }"
>
</div>
This will render as the following. 
<div>
  <b style="color: red;" >Steve</b>
  <p>Hi there!</p>
</div>

docs.title: x-contents
docs.text:
We can also pass HTML children into a designated container inside the source passage, by using x-contents on the container.

Source passage: 

:: Dialogue Box
<div>
  <b :style="{ color: nameColor }" >{{name}}</b>
  <div x-contents></div>
</div>
Usage with x-passage: 
<div
  x-passage="'Dialogue Box'"
  x-data="{
    name: 'Steve',
    nameColor: 'red'
  }"
>
  <p>Hi there!</p>
  <p>The weather is great right now. Let's go for a walk.</p>
</div>
Renders as: 
<div>
  <b style="color: red;" >Steve</b>
  <div>
    <p>Hi there!</p>
    <p>The weather is great right now. Let's go for a walk.</p>
  </div>
</div>
